corrections.baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream operator>> and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int> (cpp/src/words.cpp; g++ 16 and clang++ 22, libstdc++); best C/C++ row is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s. The C rows (c/src/words.c) strdup the whole text per iteration, tokenize with strtok_r and count in uthash with a malloc plus strdup per distinct word, at about 1.96-2.0 s.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Rust 1.021 s vs C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s (best of the 16 C/C++ configurations), C++/G++/Unsafe 1.631 s, C++/G++ 1.638 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s (-O3 -march=native) and C/Clang 1.988 s: about 1.55x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.60x faster than C++/G++ prod (derived from page data). Peak RSS 5.4 MB (C++ 7.8 MB). Other rows also beat every C/C++ row: Crystal 0.88 s, Zig 0.91 s, Go 1.129 s, Rust/PGO 0.898 s. Earlier monthly runs show a smaller Rust lead over the best C/C++ row: 1.18x on 2026-08-14 (1.37 vs 1.623 s), 1.21x on 2026-09-03 (1.329 vs 1.613 s), 1.53x on 2026-09-18 (1.054 vs 1.612 s); the jump followed the 2026-09-06 commit 'rust: count Words with borrowed &str keys' (derived from the results files).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (c/Makefile, cpp/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag), -std=c++20 for C++. Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3, no -march). 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -fvisibility=hidden -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) appear only in LDFLAGS while objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO rows were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Rust: rustc 1.99.0, 'cargo build --release' with the default release profile (opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu flag; rust/Cargo.toml).

corrections.workload: Split a generated 50,000-word text (words of 3 to 8 random lowercase letters separated by single spaces) into words, count frequencies in a hash map, then fold the top word, its count and the vocabulary size into a checksum; 360 timed iterations, text generation untimed.
corrections.why_faster: Standard-library and idiom differences, not code generation (from the sources): Rust iterates split_whitespace() and keys a HashMap (SwissTable, default SipHash-1-3) with &str slices borrowed from the text, so no key is copied; C++ extracts each word through std::istringstream operator>> (stream sentry and per-character locale whitespace checks) into a std::string (3-8 chars, inside libstdc++'s small-string buffer) and std::unordered_map allocates one node per distinct word, and nearly every word is distinct. Before the borrowed-key change Rust used owned keys and led by only about 1.2x.
corrections.caveats: Standard-library and idiom comparison (istringstream tokenizer plus node-based unordered_map against a borrowed-slice tokenizer and an open-addressing map), not code generation; a C++ version with std::string_view keys and a flat hash map would likely close the gap. Half the current margin comes from the 2026-09-06 Rust change to borrowed &str keys (1.2x before, 1.55x after). The C version does extra work (strdup of the whole text each iteration, malloc plus strdup per distinct word). The same test appears under Java in the wave jitaot file. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance reported), although the harness checks each run's checksum against run.js. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows also lose. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked as text tests where a non-C row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests go the other way (Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust; Distance::Jaro is a tie).

notes: Confirm at A: numbers match the 2026-10-05 results file exactly and metadata checks out (MIT, 41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, not a fork, not archived). Shortcomings to record: idiom and container comparison rather than a language win; margin rose from 1.2x to 1.55x after the Rust test switched to borrowed keys on 2026-09-06; C++ code uses istringstream and std::string keys where string_view keys would remove copies; single run; subjective, AI-assisted suite.

corrections.workload: Parse a generated 100,000-row CSV (70 timed iterations, generation untimed) whose quoted text columns contain commas, doubled quotes and a literal backslash-n character pair (no embedded line breaks), extract three unquoted float columns per row (fields 1, 3 and 5) and average them.
corrections.why_faster: Library differences, not the language (from the sources): the Zig test uses the third-party csv-zero field iterator, which its README describes as zero-allocation and SIMD-accelerated, and std.fmt.parseFloat (an Eisel-Lemire style parser); the C test scans byte by byte and calls glibc strtod, and the C++ test uses lazycsv and std::stod on a std::string copy of each cell. How much comes from field scanning versus float parsing was not measured.
corrections.caveats: Library comparison: the suite pins a different CSV parser per language (README: 'for library-based (JSON, Base64, CSV), I use the best practical option for each language'), SIMD csv-zero for Zig against a scalar hand-written C loop and lazycsv for C++, with different float parsers, so the result says nothing about Zig code generation; a C/C++ build with a SIMD CSV scanner and fast_float would be the fair comparison. The workload has no multi-line fields (the '\\n' in the generator is a literal backslash and n). The Zig prod build is ReleaseSafe with safety checks on and presumably host-CPU code generation (inference), against generic x86-64 C/C++ prod builds; the -march=native C/C++ rows still lose. The sibling Rust row of this test is in the wave sys file (batch-29, tier C). LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance reported), although the harness checks each run's checksum against run.js. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows also lose. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked as text tests where a non-C row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests go the other way (Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust; Distance::Jaro is a tie).

corrections.workload: For 10 generated string pairs (lengths 4 to 20,003 over a 10-letter alphabet), pack each 4-gram into a u32, count grams of the first string in one hash map and of the second in another while counting the intersection, and sum the overlap scores; 100 timed iterations.
corrections.why_faster: Container differences, not code generation (inference from the sources): Zig's std.AutoHashMap(u32,u32) is an open-addressing table with flat key and value arrays, while std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> allocates a node per distinct gram (up to 10,000 per map with a 10-letter alphabet) and maps the identity hash to a prime bucket count; the test builds and frees two maps per string pair. Zig wins even with ReleaseSafe runtime checks on (ReleaseFast is 0.325 s).
corrections.caveats: Container comparison: a C++ open-addressing map (absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map) would likely close the gap, and the suite only uses std::unordered_map (the C rows use uthash with a malloc per gram and are about 2x slower still). The Zig prod build is ReleaseSafe and presumably targets the host CPU (inference from zig/build.zig) against generic x86-64 C/C++ prod builds; the -march=native C/C++ rows still lose. Rust, C#, Go and others also beat C++ here, so the result is about std::unordered_map, not Zig. The C# row of this test is in the wave jitaot file. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance reported), although the harness checks each run's checksum against run.js. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows also lose. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked as text tests where a non-C row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests go the other way (Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust; Distance::Jaro is a tie).

notes: Confirm at A: numbers match the Distance::NGram-runtime entries and the lead has held at 1.4-1.6x across four monthly runs; metadata checks out (MIT, 41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08). Shortcomings to record: a std::unordered_map versus open-addressing map comparison rather than a language win (Rust, C#, Go also win); single run per configuration; subjective, AI-assisted suite; headline C++ rows at -O2, though -O3 and PGO rows also lose; LTO flags inert.
